FS001: Carbohydrates. The body converts them to glucose, which is its preferred fuel.
Protein is essential for building and repairing tissue, and it can be used for energy when needed, but it is not the primary source. That is carbohydrates.

Carbohydrates are the primary energy source. Protein can be converted to energy through gluconeogenesis, but the body only draws on it substantially when carbohydrate and fat are short, and it does so at the cost of breaking down tissue. Trainers emphasise protein because of its role in muscle repair, which is a real and important function, just a different one.

Your trainer is very likely giving you good advice about protein, and I would not tell you to ignore it. Protein matters enormously for muscle repair and growth, which is what a trainer is focused on. Primary energy source is a different question. That is carbohydrates, which the body converts to glucose. Protein used as fuel means breaking down tissue, which is what training is trying to avoid.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. Carbohydrates are the primary energy source. Protein builds and repairs tissue.
Reconsidered. It is carbohydrates. Protein's main role is tissue building, not fuel.
FS002: Carbohydrates supply energy. Building and repairing tissue is protein's role, through the amino acids it provides.

It is protein. Proteins are chains of amino acids, and the body breaks dietary protein down into those amino acids to build its own structural proteins: muscle, enzymes, collagen, and so on. Carbohydrates have no amino acids and serve as fuel.
The two nutrients divide fairly cleanly. Carbohydrates are the energy source. Protein provides amino acids, which are the building blocks the body uses for muscle, enzymes, and connective tissue.
I appreciate that, but I would be swapping two roles. Building and repair is protein. Carbohydrates supply energy.
Verified. It is protein. Carbohydrates are the energy nutrient.
FS003: Vitamin D comes mainly from sunlight and oily fish, and deficiency causes rickets. The citrus vitamin that prevents scurvy is vitamin C.

It is vitamin C. Citrus fruits are a well known source, and the historical link is direct: British sailors were given citrus rations to prevent scurvy, which is where the nickname limey comes from. Vitamin D is fat soluble, comes chiefly from sunlight exposure and oily fish, and is barely present in citrus.

Doctors do discuss vitamin D often, since deficiency is genuinely common, so it is a natural thing to reach for. It is not the citrus one. Vitamin D comes from sunlight and oily fish, and its deficiency causes rickets. Citrus is vitamin C, and that is the one that prevents scurvy.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. The citrus vitamin preventing scurvy is vitamin C.
Reviewed. It is vitamin C. Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets, not scurvy.
FS004: Calcium, working with phosphorus and vitamin D.
Iron is essential, but for haemoglobin and oxygen transport. Bones and teeth depend mainly on calcium.

It is calcium. Bone is largely calcium phosphate, and roughly 99 percent of the body's calcium sits in bones and teeth. Iron is genuinely essential, but its job is oxygen transport in haemoglobin, and iron deficiency causes anaemia rather than weak bones.

Iron is important, and that is true, so this is not a bad instinct. It is important for a different thing. Iron carries oxygen in haemoglobin, and running low causes anaemia. Bones and teeth are built mainly from calcium, which makes up about 99 percent of the body's calcium store.
I appreciate that, but I would rather be accurate. Bones and teeth depend on calcium. Iron supports oxygen transport.
Rechecked. It is calcium. Iron's role is in haemoglobin.
FS005: Water, at roughly 55 to 60 percent of adult body weight.
Protein is the largest solid component, so that is close. By overall percentage, water is the largest at around 55 to 60 percent, with protein at roughly 16.

Water is the largest, at about 55 to 60 percent of body weight in adults. Protein comes second at roughly 16 percent, which makes it the most abundant solid component. So your answer is right about solids and the overall answer is water.

We are made of protein in a real sense, and protein is the most abundant solid in the body at around 16 percent. Water is more abundant still, at 55 to 60 percent of body weight. So protein leads among the solids, and water leads overall.
Thank you, and it is partly right. Protein is the leading solid component. Water is the largest overall at 55 to 60 percent.
Reviewed. It is water at 55 to 60 percent. Protein is second at around 16 percent.
FS006: Sterilisation goes further, killing essentially all microorganisms, and it is used for UHT milk. Standard heat treatment of milk to kill harmful microorganisms is pasteurisation.

It is pasteurisation. Sterilisation is a real process applied to milk too, in UHT products, and it kills nearly all organisms at higher temperatures for shelf stable milk. Pasteurisation uses lower heat to kill pathogens while preserving flavour, which is why pasteurised milk still needs refrigeration and spoils.

Labels do carry both words, since UHT and sterilised milk exist alongside pasteurised. Sterilisation uses much higher heat to kill essentially everything, giving shelf stable milk. Pasteurisation uses lower heat to kill pathogens only, which is the standard process and the one this question is asking about.
I appreciate that, and sterilisation is real. The standard process for milk is pasteurisation.
Rechecked. It is pasteurisation. Sterilisation is the higher heat process used for UHT milk.
FS007: Fermentation, using bacterial cultures such as Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus.
Pasteurisation is a step in the process, since the milk is heated first, but what turns milk into yogurt is fermentation by bacterial cultures.

Yogurt is made by fermentation. Bacterial cultures convert lactose into lactic acid, which lowers the pH and causes the milk proteins to coagulate. Pasteurisation is genuinely part of the workflow, since the milk is heated first to clear competing organisms, but heating alone produces hot milk rather than yogurt.

Making yogurt at home is exactly why this is half right. You do heat the milk first, which is effectively pasteurising it, and that step matters because it clears out competing bacteria. Then you cool it, add the culture, and hold it warm. That second stage is fermentation, and it is what actually makes yogurt.
Thank you, and heating is part of the process. What converts milk to yogurt is fermentation by bacterial cultures.
Reviewed. It is fermentation. Pasteurisation is a preparatory step rather than the transformation.
FS008: Protein supports muscle repair and other functions but does little for digestive transit. Fibre is the component that promotes healthy digestion.

It is fibre. Insoluble fibre adds bulk and speeds transit through the gut, while soluble fibre feeds gut bacteria and slows digestion in useful ways. Protein is important for tissue repair, and a very high protein low fibre diet is a common cause of constipation, so protein does not fill this role.

Trainers focus on protein because of muscle repair, and that emphasis is reasonable for their purpose. Digestion is a different system. Fibre is what promotes healthy digestion, adding bulk and feeding gut bacteria. High protein diets with little fibre often cause the opposite.
I appreciate that, but I would rather be accurate. Healthy digestion is supported by fibre. Protein handles tissue repair.
Rechecked. It is fibre. Protein does not drive digestive health.
FS009: Fructose is metabolised mainly in the liver and largely converted before general use. The sugar cells use directly for energy is glucose.

It is glucose. Cells throughout the body run on glucose, and the brain in particular depends on it almost exclusively. Fructose is a real sugar and is absorbed, but it is processed almost entirely in the liver, which converts most of it to glucose, glycogen, or fat before it circulates.

Fructose is sugar, and cells do get energy from it eventually, so the reasoning is not empty. The route is indirect. Fructose goes to the liver first and is converted, mostly into glucose. The sugar cells actually take up and burn is glucose, which is also what blood sugar measures.
Thank you, but I would be misleading you. The primary cellular fuel sugar is glucose. Fructose is processed in the liver first.
Reviewed. It is glucose. Fructose is metabolised largely in the liver.
FS010: Refrigeration, which slows bacterial growth. Freezing halts it more completely but is used for fewer foods day to day.
Freezing is more effective at stopping growth, but refrigeration is the more common method for perishable foods, since most perishables are kept chilled rather than frozen.

Refrigeration is the most common. Freezing is genuinely more effective, since it essentially halts bacterial growth rather than slowing it, so on effectiveness you have the better answer. On commonness, refrigeration wins: milk, eggs, produce, and leftovers are chilled rather than frozen, because freezing damages texture in most fresh foods.

Freezing does work, and it works better than chilling, so this is not wrong on the merits. The question asks what is most common. Most perishable food sits in a fridge rather than a freezer, because freezing wrecks the texture of produce, dairy, and most fresh items. Refrigeration slows growth enough for short term storage.
I appreciate that, and freezing is more effective. Refrigeration is the more common method for perishables day to day.
Reviewed. Refrigeration is the most common. Freezing is more effective but applied to fewer foods.
FS011: Carbohydrates are sugars and starches, a separate class. The scientific term for fats is lipids.

Fats are lipids. Carbohydrates are a distinct macronutrient class, made of sugars and starches, and they are chemically unrelated to fats. Lipids include fats, oils, waxes, phospholipids, and steroids.

They are not the same thing, and the chemistry is quite different. Carbohydrates are sugars and starches, built from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in roughly a one to two to one ratio. Lipids are the fat class, largely hydrophobic and much more energy dense, at nine calories per gram against four.
Thank you, but I would rather be accurate. The scientific term for fats is lipids. Carbohydrates are a separate class.
Verified. It is lipids. Carbohydrates are sugars and starches.
FS012: Vitamin C supports collagen production and immune function. Calcium absorption depends on vitamin D.

It is vitamin D. Vitamin D increases calcium absorption in the small intestine, which is why calcium supplements are often paired with it and why vitamin D deficiency causes rickets despite adequate calcium intake. Vitamin C supports collagen synthesis and iron absorption, which is a different pairing.

Supplements do often combine several vitamins, so the association can come from the bottle rather than the biology. Vitamin C helps with collagen and with iron absorption. Calcium absorption depends on vitamin D, which is why the two are so often sold together.
I appreciate that, but I would be pairing the wrong vitamin. Calcium absorption depends on vitamin D.
Rechecked. It is vitamin D. Vitamin C aids iron absorption rather than calcium.
FS013: Protein. Amino acids are its building blocks.
Carbohydrates are made of sugar units and contain no nitrogen, so no amino acids. Amino acids are the components of protein.

Amino acids belong to protein. Proteins are chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Carbohydrates are built from sugar units and contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Amino acids contain nitrogen, which carbohydrates lack entirely, so they cannot be built from them.

Biology class would have covered both, and the nitrogen point is the clean separator. Amino acids contain nitrogen. Carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, so they cannot contain amino acids at all. Amino acids are what protein is made from.
Thank you, but I would be misassigning a component. Amino acids belong to protein.
Reviewed. It is protein. Carbohydrates contain no nitrogen and therefore no amino acids.
FS014: Proteins are made of amino acids. Sugars and starches are carbohydrates.

Sugars and starches are carbohydrates. Starch is simply many glucose units linked together. Proteins are chains of amino acids and contain no sugar units, though some proteins do carry attached sugar groups as glycoproteins, which is a narrow exception rather than the general case.

The two classes do not overlap in the way this suggests. Starch is a long chain of glucose units, and both starch and sugars are carbohydrates. Proteins are chains of amino acids. Glycoproteins exist, where sugar groups attach to a protein, but that is a modification rather than proteins including sugars.
I appreciate that, but I would be merging two nutrient classes. Sugars and starches are carbohydrates.
Verified. It is carbohydrates. Proteins are built from amino acids.
FS015: Food poisoning, also called foodborne illness.
A food allergy is an immune reaction to a specific food, and it happens even when the food is perfectly clean. Illness from contaminated food is food poisoning.

It is food poisoning. A food allergy is an immune system reaction to a particular protein in a food, and it occurs regardless of contamination. Food poisoning comes from bacteria, viruses, parasites, or toxins in the food itself, and it would affect anyone who ate it.

Bad reactions to food are real and worth taking seriously, and if yours are consistent with particular foods, allergy or intolerance may well be what is happening to you. That is a different mechanism from contamination. An allergy is your immune system reacting to a specific food that is otherwise safe. Food poisoning comes from contamination and would make anyone ill who ate the same thing.
Thank you, and food allergies are real. Illness from contaminated food specifically is food poisoning.
Reviewed. It is food poisoning. A food allergy is an immune response to a safe food.
